pages.x: In December 2019 doctors in Wuhan, a Chinese city of 11 million, saw patients with a pneumonia nobody could explain. It was a new coronavirus. A young eye doctor, Li Wenliang, warned friends in a chat group, and the police made him sign a confession for spreading rumours. He died of the disease in February.

On 23 January 2020 China sealed Wuhan off from the world, but the virus had already spread. In March, as Italy's hospitals were overwhelmed, the World Health Organization declared a pandemic. Within weeks half of humanity had been told to stay at home, the biggest lockdown in history.

Schools, offices, shops and stadiums closed. Planes stood on the ground, and wild animals wandered into empty cities. Children learned at home on screens, people worked over video calls, and families said goodbye to dying relatives on phones. Doctors and nurses worked in masks for months on end, and many caught the virus and died.

By 2024 more than seven million deaths had been reported to the WHO, and the true number, counting deaths that were never recorded, was perhaps two or three times higher. The old and the sick were most at risk. The United States counted more dead than any other country, over a million.
Scientists built vaccines in less than a year, a task that used to take a decade. Some used messenger RNA, a new method that teaches the body's own cells to make a harmless piece of the virus.
pages.fx: In December 2020 Margaret Keenan, a 90-year-old grandmother in Coventry, became the first person to get the Pfizer vaccine once it was approved. Billions of doses followed, saving millions of lives.

pages.x: The virus kept changing. In the spring of 2021 the Delta variant tore through India, where hospitals ran out of oxygen and cremation fires burned through the night. Then came Omicron, which spread faster still but was milder. Poorer countries waited months for vaccines that richer ones had bought up.

On 5 May 2023 the WHO declared that Covid-19 was no longer a global health emergency. The virus has not gone away, but vaccines and earlier infections have made it far less deadly. Where it came from, an animal at a city market or an accident at a laboratory, is still argued over.

The pandemic was the worst since the Spanish flu of 1918. It changed how people work, set back millions of children at school, and left many with long Covid. It also showed how fast science can move when the whole world needs it.
pts: First found in Wuhan, China, at the end of 2019
Vaccines were made in less than a year
